content:
Major repair scaffolding increases the risk of burglary for units. Some contractors have installed CCTV on scaffolding that extends over the pavement, with cameras pointing at passers-by.

At least 11 buildings in Sham Shui Po and Cheung Sha Wan have CCTV on scaffolding, some filming the pavement

Streets in Sham Shui Po and Cheung Sha Wan have many old buildings, and it is common to see scaffolding erected for repair works. The Collective recently observed that at least 11 buildings in the area undergoing major repair works have CCTV installed on their scaffolding, ranging from a single camera to as many as six. Some cameras only film the area near the building entrances, while others film back alleys. However, many cameras face the pavement, capturing passers-by.

CCTV installed on scaffolding extending over the pavement means passers-by may inadvertently become subjects of surveillance.

Some buildings have notices posted at their entrances stating that CCTV surveillance is in operation.

Owners' corporation chairman: burglaries occurred after scaffolding was erected, CCTV added as a precaution

Why install CCTV on scaffolding? A worker on a building on Cheung Sha Wan Road said the reason was to "prevent theft" — "afraid people would climb up and steal things." Another building on Un Chau Street, which also has CCTV on its scaffolding, has a notice posted in the stairwell stating that since repair works began, there have been two burglary cases in residential units. The building's owners' corporation chairman, Mr. Wan, said burglaries occurred shortly after the scaffolding was erected, "so the construction company felt that, for safety's sake, they added some CCTV."

Scaffolding extending onto the pavement effectively means CCTV has been installed on the pavement as part of the repair works.

CCTV successfully caught a thief stealing lightning conductors

A building on Wong Chuk Street also has CCTV installed on its scaffolding. A staff member of the works contractor, Sing Kee Engineering, Mr. Wu, further revealed that since installation, they had already "caught a thief." "A thief went to steal lightning conductors to sell. Because there was CCTV, we could see the thief up there." He said that to ensure security during the building's repair works, installing CCTV to film the scaffolding area was standard practice: "to make sure that if any strangers or anyone climbs onto the scaffolding, security is notified immediately, and they go catch them."

A building on Wong Chuk Street also has CCTV installed on its scaffolding. A staff member of the works contractor, Sing Kee Engineering, Mr. Wu, further revealed that since installation, they had already "caught a thief."

Most did not follow the Privacy Commissioner's guidelines in posting notices; only one building had a notice

According to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data's "Guidance on the Use of CCTV Monitoring," data users should clearly inform individuals who may be affected that they are under CCTV surveillance. One effective method is to place prominent notices within the monitored area. However, based on the reporter's on-site observations, of the 11 buildings, four only had pre-existing notices at their entrances such as "CCTV filming nearby" or "24-hour CCTV installed here," while another six had no notices visible at the building entrances or perimeter at all, including two buildings on Un Chau Street and Wong Chuk Street.

A building on Castle Peak Road in Cheung Sha Wan was the only one to place prominent notices within the monitored area, including on the scaffolding near the cameras. Some of these notices also listed the data user's information in accordance with the Guidance, stating that the CCTV is managed by Tin Yik (Group) Construction Limited, with a contact phone number provided for enquiries about personal data handling.

Of the 11 buildings the reporter inspected with CCTV installed within the pavement area, only one had a prominent warning notice near the cameras.

A Mr. Chow from the company replied to enquiries that CCTV was installed out of concern that people would climb the scaffolding, to prevent trespassers from breaking in and to give police more information for investigations: "Actually we just want to let the thieves know to give up — pick somewhere easier, don't pick this place." He said that before installation they had communicated with the building's owners' corporation, consultants, and the ground-floor gold shop, which had experience with CCTV and reminded them that notices had to be posted to inform the public. The consultants gave the same advice: "afraid people might mistake it for private use."

Most passers-by don't mind being filmed: "There's not much privacy on the street anyway"

Passers-by walking past may be captured on CCTV. Most passers-by did not notice the CCTV, but generally said they did not mind, though some felt posting notices would be better. Mr. Lee said outright: "There's not much privacy on the street anyway." He was not worried about privacy issues from CCTV: "It's perfectly normal — lots of shops have them too." He thought having notices was a good thing, but if there were none, "it's only up for a while, no problem. It's not like it'll be there for years — once the work is done, it's taken down."

Walking on the street, have you noticed that you are already living under the gaze of CCTV cameras?

An elderly man who did not wish to be named also said: "There are more and more cameras these days, where is there any privacy? Right?" Regarding the cameras, he said as long as it's not illegal, he did not mind: "If you're breaking the law, of course you'd be afraid — of course that's not good!" But he added that some people might simply not want their whereabouts known. Ms. Chan, a resident who often passes through Cheung Sha Wan Road, also did not notice that one building's scaffolding had CCTV, but said she did not mind: "No problem, it's for safety." She added: "At least if a thief catches me, there's footage." Ms. Leung, also passing by, said she did not mind: "I'm only here for a minute, so they'll only film me for a minute!"

Some passers-by say notices would be better: "If you don't like it, you can take a detour"

Mr. Ng had a different view: "Filming their own entrance area is actually fine — there's really no need to film the whole street." But he added that he was not a nearby resident and rarely passed by, so he was relatively less concerned. He agreed that having notices would be better: "At least you know there's a camera here, and you might be filmed. At least those who really don't want to be filmed can take a detour."

During major repairs, some construction companies have added CCTV for theft prevention.

Owners' corporation chairmen and contractors question the requirement: shops with CCTV also have no notices

Regarding CCTV filming passers-by without notices informing them of surveillance, Mr. Wan asked rhetorically: "Turning it around, lots of shops have CCTV filming the street — do they have notices? Seems like they don't." He subsequently said this issue would need to be consulted on further.

Mr. Wu similarly questioned whether notices needed to be posted: "All the CCTV around films like this — like the ones in shops, they all film like this too. Nobody said they had to post notices. I mean, when I walk into any shop, they film me like this too — and the police catch thieves through this, right?" He stressed that filming in public places is permissible: "I don't prefer them doing whatever there, but we're just protecting our own property." He added that if requested, they could also post notices: "We don't mind — we're just protecting the owners' corporation, just protecting the service users."

Privacy Commissioner reminds that purpose must be stated; data subjects may request access

The Office of the Privacy Commissioner replied to The Collective's enquiry without commenting on individual cases. The office reminded building owners or works contractors that if CCTV systems installed on scaffolding have recording functions capable of capturing and storing images or footage of others, for the purpose of identifying those individuals or compiling information about specific individuals, this may constitute the collection of "personal data" and must comply with the Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance and its six data protection principles.

The office further stated that, among other requirements, personal data must be collected for a lawful purpose directly related to the function or activity of the data user, must be collected by lawful and fair means, and all reasonably practicable steps must be taken to inform data subjects at or before the time of collection of the purpose for which the data will be used, the classes of persons to whom the data may be transferred, and the rights and channels through which data subjects may request access to and correction of their own data.

CCTV cameras point at areas with scaffolding for major repairs, for theft prevention purposes.

CCTV without recording function activated does not constitute collecting "personal data"; Privacy Ordinance does not apply

The office further reminded owners or contractors that unless they have obtained the voluntary and explicit consent of data subjects, the use, disclosure, and transfer of personal data should only be for the purpose stated at the time of collection or purposes directly related thereto. As for CCTV without the recording function activated, the office stated that installing such a system does not involve the collection of "personal data" and the relevant provisions of the Privacy Ordinance do not apply.

Buildings under repair have installed CCTV on the pavement — some members of the public feel it's no big deal, while others believe warning notices should be posted in prominent locations.

Lawyer: exemption from notice requirement possible if it would prejudice crime detection

Lawyer Chan Pak-ho told The Collective that the Privacy Ordinance requires that the method of collecting personal data should be notified to the data subject — for example, posting a notice to inform people that CCTV is collecting facial images here. Failure to post a notice may violate the data protection principles of the Ordinance. However, he also pointed out that in cases of preventing or detecting crime, if posting notices would prejudice the purpose of crime detection, the Ordinance provides for an exemption: "Because if we post these notices, it might let people who want to break the law know that they shouldn't commit crime here, but should do it somewhere else — that could undermine the purpose of detecting crime." He believed that in certain circumstances, installing CCTV without a notice does not necessarily violate the data protection principles of the Ordinance.

Chan Pak-ho said that if the Privacy Commissioner issues an enforcement notice to a building management office in this regard, requiring rectification of the breach of data protection principles within a specified period, failure to comply would constitute an offence punishable by fine and imprisonment. As for the placement of notices, he said posting at the building entrance would be sufficient, but it should clearly state that CCTV is not only at the building entrance and lobby but throughout the entire building — including on the scaffolding — to better meet legal requirements.

A building has a CCTV warning notice posted at its entrance.

Lawyer reminds to avoid filming residents; high-definition filming of streets without notices may violate the law

Chan Pak-ho reminded that if a building wishes to install CCTV on scaffolding, it should avoid filming inside residential units of that building or other buildings, as this would clearly violate residents' privacy: "Of course I understand there may be practical difficulties — on one hand wanting a clear view of the entire scaffolding, and on the other afraid of filming into residents' units. Indeed, this requires very skilful angle adjustment."

As for filming streets, Chan said public places are not private spaces, and it can be reasonably expected that people may not have high expectations of personal privacy there. However, if the footage is very high-definition, attention is needed: "If it's very high-definition — meaning people walking by on the street, and their faces are being collected by CCTV somewhere, and at the same time there's no relevant notice given to them — then under such circumstances, it may violate the data collection principle under the Ordinance."

Among the CCTV on scaffolding, products from Zhejiang Dahua Technology Co., Ltd. are a popular brand — at least 8 of the 11 buildings' scaffolding use them. The company was placed on the US Commerce Department's Entity List in 2019.

A garage has also installed CCTV on the street, for the purpose of preventing police from issuing parking tickets.

CCTV positioned directly at areas where passers-by walk.
